analysis.one_liner: Restructures the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau under a five-member commission and subjects its funding to annual congressional appropriations.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee advanced the bill on a 26-23 party-line vote in December 2023, but it never received a vote by the full House before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau — the agency that writes and enforces rules for mortgages, credit cards, debt collection, and credit reports — out of the Federal Reserve and make it a standalone agency run by a five-person commission instead of one director. It would end the bureau's automatic funding from the Federal Reserve and require Congress to approve its money each year, capped at $650 million for fiscal 2024, while sweeping an equal amount out of the fund that holds penalties paid by rule-breaking companies. It would also require the bureau to publish detailed cost-benefit studies before issuing rules, examine the impact on small businesses, give the bureau its own inspector general, and pay awards to whistleblowers whose tips lead to penalties.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, payday lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting companies that are regulated and regularly fined by the CFPB. A commission with staggered terms, private-sector experience requirements, and a funding stream Congress controls annually would slow rulemaking and make enforcement easier to stall. Whistleblowers who report financial misconduct would also gain a new award program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, payday lenders, debt collectors, credit bureaus

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the CFPB's single director with a five-member commission appointed by the President, with no more than three members from one party and at least two required to have private-sector experience in consumer financial products.

Ends the bureau's funding through Federal Reserve transfers and puts it under the regular appropriations process, authorizing $650 million for fiscal year 2024 — and on appropriation, transfers an equal amount out of the Consumer Financial Civil Penalty Fund to the Treasury.

Requires the bureau to publish, with every proposed rule, quantitative cost-benefit analysis, alternatives considered, effects on consumer access to credit, and justification if costs outweigh benefits.
Requires detailed analysis of each rule's impact on small businesses, with consultation with the Small Business Administration when small firms would bear added costs.
Gives the CFPB its own inspector general, separate from the Federal Reserve's inspector general, and requires semiannual testimony to Congress.

Creates a whistleblower award program paying 10 to 30 percent of monetary sanctions (capped at $5 million per person) to people whose original information leads to enforcement actions over $1 million.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who use credit. The bureau's rules cover overdraft and credit card fees, mortgage servicing, debt collection, and credit reporting; a slower, smaller bureau with divided leadership would issue fewer rules and bring fewer enforcement actions, and penalties paid by violators would be redirected from the fund that compensates victims to the general Treasury.

drawbacks.text: Subjecting the CFPB to annual appropriations makes its budget a bargaining chip each year; Congress could effectively zero it out, unlike the current Federal Reserve transfer designed to insulate it from industry pressure.

A five-member commission with staggered vacancies can deadlock, leaving the main consumer finance regulator unable to act for long stretches — the reason Congress originally created a single director after the 2008 financial crisis.

The bill sweeps an equal amount out of the Consumer Financial Civil Penalty Fund each time the bureau is appropriated, redirecting penalties paid by companies that broke the law away from the fund used to compensate harmed consumers.

Requiring quantified cost-benefit analysis for every rule can stall protections whose benefits — prevented fraud, discrimination, and abusive collection — are real but hard to express as dollars, and lets regulated companies litigate over the paperwork.

Supporters argue the current CFPB is uniquely unaccountable: it is funded outside the normal appropriations process and run by one unelected director, and a separate inspector general and published cost-benefit analysis would bring transparency other agencies already face.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains genuinely defensible accountability ideas — a dedicated inspector general, published cost-benefit analysis, and whistleblower awards are features of other regulators. But its central changes — replacing the director with a commission and moving funding to annual appropriations with a $650 million cap and a parallel sweep from the penalties fund — would structurally weaken the one agency whose sole job is policing consumer finance, and the paperwork requirements would give regulated companies new ways to delay rules in court. The whistleblower title cuts the other way and would strengthen enforcement. On net, the bill's main effect would be to slow and shrink consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: The Financial Services Committee voted the bill out 26-23 in April 2023 and formally reported it to the House floor in December 2023, but House leadership never scheduled a floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr introduced the bill on April 24, 2023, and it was referred to the Financial Services, Oversight, Judiciary, and Small Business Committees.
On April 26, 2023, the Financial Services Committee ordered the bill reported on a 26-23 roll-call vote.
The committee formally reported the bill on December 4, 2023, the other three committees were discharged, and it was placed on the Union Calendar — the list of bills awaiting a House floor vote.
The bill never received a vote in the full House, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill under the rule that unfinished legislation expires.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers of mortgages, credit cards, and loans keep the CFPB's current structure and funding, because the bill that would have restructured it never reached the House floor. Regulated lenders and collectors did not get the changes they sought, and victims' compensation from the civil penalties fund was not redirected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers who keep the current CFPB

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.role: U.S. Representative, KY-6; chair of the Financial Services Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Monetary Policy
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and steered it through the Financial Services Committee, which reported it to the House floor.

for.name: Reps. Erin Houchin and Riley Moore Hunt
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only two cosponsors in December 2023 when it was reported.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee Republicans
for.role: Committee majority that controlled the markup
for.what_they_did: Voted 26-23 on party lines to report the bill, and reported it to the House floor in December 2023.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee Democrats
against.what_they_did: Provided all 23 votes against reporting the bill in the committee markup.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and leadership team controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a vote after it was placed on the Union Calendar in December 2023; it sat for over a year until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote, the 26-23 committee vote to report the bill, split entirely on party lines, with Republicans in favor and Democrats opposed; both cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on.

industries.note: The CFPB writes and enforces rules on overdraft fees, credit card late fees, and mortgage servicing that cost these firms; a commission structure and annually appropriated funding would slow that work. Because the bill died, they keep the current regulator as is.
These lenders are frequent targets of CFPB enforcement; a weaker, slower bureau with cost-benefit documentation requirements would reduce the rules and fines they face.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: The CFPB polices debt collection and credit reporting practices that affect millions of consumers; restructuring and defunding channels would ease pressure on both industries.

industries.industry: Whistleblowers and plaintiffs in financial misconduct cases
industries.note: The bill's whistleblower title pays 10-30 percent of sanctions to people whose tips lead to enforcement — the one provision that would strengthen policing of financial firms.
